'''Raymond Freeman''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Keeler |first=James |last2=Morris |first2=Gareth A. |date=2024 |title=Ray Freeman. 6 January 1932—1 May 2022 |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsbm.2023.0026 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=76}}</ref> (6 January 1932 – 1 May 2022) was a British chemist and academic, who was a professor at [[Jesus College, Cambridge]] and made important contributions to [[Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|NMR spectroscopy]].<ref name="googlescholar">{{GoogleScholar|id=4dDMfAoAAAAJ}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ch.cam.ac.uk/staff/rf.html|title=Cambridge University: Professor Ray Freeman|accessdate=2008-12-06 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080611140310/http://www.ch.cam.ac.uk/staff/rf.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 2008-06-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www-jmg.ch.cam.ac.uk/oldchem/staff/rf.html|title = Raven login}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1021/ja00497a058| title = Enhancement of nuclear magnetic resonance signals by polarization transfer| journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society| volume = 101| issue = 3| pages = 760| year = 1979| last1 = Morris | first1 = G. A. | last2 = Freeman | first2 = R. }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/0022-2364(85)90122-2| title = Computer-optimized decoupling scheme for wideband applications and low-level operation| journal = Journal of Magnetic Resonance| volume = 64| issue = 3| pages = 547| year = 1985| last1 = Shaka | first1 = A. J. | last2 = Barker | first2 = P. B. | last3 = Freeman | first3 = R. | bibcode = 1985JMagR..64..547S}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/0022-2364(81)90287-0| title = Investigation of complex networks of spin-spin coupling by two-dimensional NMR| journal = Journal of Magnetic Resonance| volume = 44| issue = 3| pages = 542| year = 1981| last1 = Bax | first1 = A. | last2 = Freeman | first2 = R. | bibcode = 1981JMagR..44..542B}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Freeman was born in [[Long Eaton]], [[Derbyshire]] on 6 January 1932.<ref name="ODNB">{{cite web |title=Freeman, Raymond [Ray] |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/display/10.1093/odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-90000382725?rskey=jtHPbE&result=98 |website=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |access-date=8 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="whoswho">{{cite web |url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U16447 |title=FREEMAN, Prof. Raymond |work=Who's Who 2014, A & C Black, an imprint of Bloomsbury Publishing plc, 2014; online edn, Oxford University Press }}{{subscription required}}</ref> He was educated at [[Nottingham High School]] in [[Nottingham|Nottingham, England]] where he won an Open Scholarship to [[Lincoln College, Oxford]] in December 1949. At the instigation of Lincoln College, he deferred his admission to Oxford to complete his military service in the [[Royal Air Force]] as a radar instructor and reached the rank of acting corporal, un-paid.

In October 1951 he returned to Oxford and began his studies in chemistry under the tutorship of [[Rex Richards (chemist)|Rex Richards]] working in research in Rex's group on NMR of the less-common nuclei (in particular [[Isotopes of cobalt|<sup>59</sup>Co]]). He earned a [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin)|Master of Arts]] and [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degrees.

==Career==
Joining the magnetic resonance group of [[Anatole Abragam]] at [[Saclay|Saclay, France]] in 1957, Freeman did [[postdoctoral research]] under the direction of an NMR pioneer [[Robert Pound]] who was on leave from [[Harvard University]]) on the super-regenerative oscillator. Freeman used the device to build a stable high-resolution NMR spectrometer.

===Varian Associates, California===
After three years in the Basic Physics division of the [[National Physical Laboratory (United Kingdom)|National Physical Laboratory, Teddington]] in the United Kingdom, Freeman took leave of absence in 1961 to work on double irradiation techniques with Wes Anderson at Varian Associates in [[Palo Alto, California]]. The environment proved to be very stimulating and a year was extended to twelve. The family lived in California and three of the children are still [[West Coast of the United States|West Coast]] residents. 
 
In addition to working on research at Varian on double-resonance, double-quantum effects, spin-lattice relaxation, and Fourier transformation, Freeman assisted in the development of new Varian NMR spectrometers (XL-100 and CFT-20).

===Back to Oxford===
In 1973 Freeman returned to Oxford as a university lecturer and a Fellow of Magdalen College beginning his own research group focused on high-resolution NMR methodology. He received a [[Doctor of Science]] degree in 1975{{citation needed|date=June 2014}} and was elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1979.<ref name="Raymond Freeman">{{Cite web |title=Raymond Freeman |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/raymond-freeman-11466/ |access-date=2022-05-04 |website=royalsociety.org}}</ref> 
 
With his research students at Oxford, several publications on new NMR techniques were released including work on two-dimensional NMR. Freeman acknowledged that part of the work was triggered by the seminal suggestion of [[Jean Jeener]] at a meeting in [[Brussels]].

===A Handbook of Magnetic Resonance===
On a short sabbatical at [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech) in [[Pasadena, California|Pasadena]], Freeman published "A Handbook of Magnetic Resonance" (translated into [[Japanese language|Japanese]] and [[Russian language|Russian]]).<ref name="handbook">{{cite book |author=Ray Freeman |title=A Handbook of Nuclear Magnetic Resonance |publisher=Longman  |year=1987  |isbn=0-582-25184-2 }}</ref>

===Cambridge===
In 1987 Freeman moved to the [[University of Cambridge]] to take up the Plummer chair of [[magnetic resonance]] and was elected a Fellow of Jesus College. He continued his research on NMR methodology there and wrote a second book, "Spin Choreography".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Freeman |first=Ray |url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/750575664 |title=Spin choreography : basic steps in high resolution NMR |date=2011 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-850481-8 |oclc=750575664}}</ref> 
 
Freeman took statutory retirement in 1999, but continued his research with a long-time colleague Eriks Kupce, and wrote his third book, "NMR in Chemistry and Medicine", published in 2003 and later translated into Russian.

==Personal life and death==
In 1958 Freeman married Anne-Marie Périnet-Marquet<ref name="whoswho"/> (originally from  [[Haute-Savoie|Haute-Savoie, France]]) and they had five children.{{citation needed|date=June 2014}} He died from bladder cancer at a hospice in [[Cambridge]], on 1 May 2022, aged 90.<ref>{{cite web |title=Professor Ray Freeman (1932–2022) |url=https://www.jesus.cam.ac.uk/articles/professor-ray-freeman-1932-2022 |website=www.jesus.cam.ac.uk |publisher=Jesus College, Cambridge |access-date=4 May 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="ODNB"/>

==Awards and honours==
Freeman was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] (FRS) in 1979.<ref name="Raymond Freeman"/> His nomination reads: {{centered pull quote|Dr Freeman has been particularly concerned with the development of High Resolution Nuclear Magnetic Resonance since 1956. Over the years he has initiated very many of the techniques of high resolution [[Nuclear Magnetic Resonance]] which are now used routinely all over the world. He was responsible for the exploitation of double and [[Triple-resonance nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|triple resonance techniques]] for the analysis of high resolution NMR spectra and for the determination of relative signs of spin coupling constants in [[Proton NMR|proton spectra]]. His two major papers on the theory of double resonance and on the theory of spin tickling form the basis of methods used universally today. He showed how [[Carbon-13|C-13]] and other weak resonances could be observed indirectly by double resonance methods and also demonstrated the use of double quantum transitions for the assignment of NMR spectra. He then published a series of elegant papers on spin-spin and [[Spin–lattice relaxation|spin-lattice relaxation]] in high resolution spectra, demonstrated some of the earliest uses of Fourier transform spectroscopy, and pioneered the methods of measuring spin-lattice relaxation times of C-13 spectra and their use for structural purposes. Dr Freeman's work is characterised by novelty and ingenuity expressed with economy and style.<ref name="royal"/>}}

Freeman was also awarded the [[Royal Medal]] in 2002.
